'''Titus Pankey''' (November 20, 1925 – September 20, 2003)<ref>{{Cite web |title=PFC Titus Pankey Jr. (1925-2003) - Find a Grave... |url=https://www.findagrave.com/memorial/58242468/titus-pankey |access-date=2022-06-27 |website=www.findagrave.com |language=en}}</ref> was an American physicist and professor whose research specialties were [[magnetic susceptibility]] and cosmology, especially supernovae. He was the first recipient of a PhD in physics from [[Howard University]], and was one of the first 10 black recipients of a PhD in physics in the United States.<ref name=":3">{{Cite web |title=The Hinton News February 15 Page 1 |url=http://hin.stparchive.com/Archive/HIN/HIN02152011p01.php |access-date=2022-06-26 |website=hin.stparchive.com}}</ref> He has been cited as the first to suggest that [[Type Ia supernova]]e are powered by nickel-56 decay.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" />

== Early life and military service ==
Titus Pankey, Jr., was born in 1925 in [[Hinton, West Virginia]]. He grew up between Hinton and [[Charlottesville, Virginia]], where he also graduated from high school. After graduation from high school, he worked as a [[Pullman porter]] on the [[Chesapeake and Ohio Railway|Chesapeake & Ohio Railway]], and helped to fund his four sisters' college educations. He later worked in an electrophoresis lab at the [[University of Virginia Health System|University of Virginia Hospital]] in Charlottesville. He served in the [[United States Army|U.S. Army]] during the [[Korean War]] and was discharged in 1954 after completing his tour of duty.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Tribune 24 July 1954 — Virginia Chronicle: Digital Newspaper Archive |url=https://virginiachronicle.com/?a=d&d=TRB19540724.1.4&srpos=1&e=-------en-20--1--txt-txIN-%22titus+pankey%22------- |access-date=2022-06-24 |website=virginiachronicle.com}}</ref> While serving in the Army's 65th Infantry Regiment, 3rd division, Pankey earned two battle stars and the Combat Infantryman's Badge.<ref>{{cite news |title=Sixteen Students to be Inducted Into Phi Beta Kappa at Howard U |newspaper=Jackson Advocate |date=19 April 1958 |page=8 |url=https://chroniclingamerica.loc.gov/lccn/sn79000083/1958-04-19/ed-1/seq-8/ }}</ref>

== Education ==
After completing his service, Pankey attended [[Howard University]] in [[Washington, D.C.]], as an undergraduate and graduated magna cum laude<ref>{{Cite web |title=Arizona Tribune, 1962-06-15 |url=https://azmemory.azlibrary.gov/digital/collection/aztribune/id/1911/ |access-date=2022-06-26 |website=azmemory.azlibrary.gov |language=en}}</ref> with a degree in physics.  

Pankey subsequently received his master's and PhD degrees from Howard in physics, completing his doctorate in 1962.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=How Elements are Forged from Stars {{!}} Spaceaustralia |url=https://spaceaustralia.com/news/how-elements-are-forged-stars |access-date=2022-06-24 |website=spaceaustralia.com}}</ref> With the completion of his degree, Pankey became the first recipient of a physics PhD from [[Howard University]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Previous Graduates {{!}} Howard University Physics Department |url=https://physics.howard.edu/people/alumni-friends/previous-graduates |access-date=2022-09-16 |website=physics.howard.edu}}</ref> 

His dissertation advisor was [[Herman Branson]], and the title of Pankey's thesis was "Possible Thermonuclear Activities in Natural Terrestrial Minerals," submitted on 26 July 1961.<ref>{{cite news |last1=University |first1=Howard |title=1962 - Howard University Commencement Program |url=https://dh.howard.edu/hugradpro/111/ |work=Howard University Commencement Programs |date=8 June 1962 }}</ref><ref name=":2">{{cite thesis |id={{ProQuest|302073367}} |last1=Pankey |first1=Titus |date=1962 |title=POSSIBLE THERMONUCLEAR ACTIVITIES IN NATURAL TERRESTRIAL MINERALS }}</ref> Branson also advised, among others, the second Howard physics PhD holder, [[Arthur Thorpe (physicist)|Arthur Thorpe]], who received his degree two years after Pankey in 1964.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Rankins |first=Claudia M. |date=13 February 2021 |title=The Story of the Connection of the First Five Physics PhD Recipients to HBCUs |url=https://nsbp.org/blogpost/1914810/365664/February-13-2021--The-First-Five |access-date=24 June 2022 |website=National Society of Black Physicists}}</ref> Pankey's research was supported by the [[United States Geological Survey|U.S. Geological Survey]] and Frank E. Senftle, and his advisory committee composed of Branson, Sohan Singh, Louis G. Swaby, and Stanton L. Wormley.<ref name=":2" /> Wormley was then the acting dean of the graduate school at Howard.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Columbia |first=United States Congress House Committee on the District of |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=SeO41z5NCk4C&dq=stanton+l+wormley+howard&pg=RA16-PA174 |title=Hearings |date=1966 |language=en}}</ref>

In March 1958, he was one of sixteen Howard students elected to the [[Phi Beta Kappa]] honors society.<ref name=":3" /><ref>Staff, Hilltop, "The Hilltop 3-28-1958" (1958). The Hilltop: 1950-60. 53. http://dh.howard.edu/hilltop_195060/53</ref> In May 1958, he was elected into an associate membership to the [[Sigma Xi]] national science honors society.<ref>{{cite news |title=Howard University To Induct 35 Into National Honor Society In Science |newspaper=Jackson Advocate |date=17 May 1958 |page=4 |url=https://chroniclingamerica.loc.gov/lccn/sn79000083/1958-05-17/ed-1/seq-4/ }}</ref><ref>Staff, Hilltop, "The Hilltop 5-17-1958" (1958). The Hilltop: 1950-60. 56. http://dh.howard.edu/hilltop_195060/56</ref>

== Career ==
[[File:Pankey-2.tif|alt=Pankey in the U.S. Naval Research Laboratory, circa 1964|thumb|Pankey in the U.S. Naval Research Laboratory, circa 1964]]
[[File:SNIacurva.svg|alt=The radioactive decays of nickel-56 and cobalt-56 that produce a supernova visible [[light curve]]|thumb|The radioactive decays of nickel-56 and cobalt-56 that produce a supernova visible light curve]]
In his graduate thesis, Pankey investigated whether nuclear fusion in the Earth's interior is a possible source of the [[Earth's internal heat budget|Earth's internal heat]], specifically by measuring the magnetic susceptibility and iron content of rocks. While radiogenic heating in the Earth is now understood to be due to decay processes rather than fusion, Pankey's thesis is significant for including a suggestion that [[radioactive decay]] of nickel-56 is responsible for powering Type Ia supernova [[light curve]]s. Pankey speculated that the two stages of decay in the light curve are caused by radioactive nickel-56 rapidly decaying to cobalt-56 with a 6 day half-life followed by cobalt-56 decaying more slowly decaying to stable iron-56 with a 77 day half-life.<ref name=":2" /> This is the first example of the now-accepted theoretical explanation for Type Ia supernova, and his thesis includes the earliest known example of a modern Type Ia light curve.<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{cite book |last1=Longair |first1=Malcolm S. |title=The Cosmic Century: A History of Astrophysics and Cosmology |date=2006 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-0-521-47436-8 }}{{pn|date=February 2023}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Stabell |first1=Oddbjørn Engvold Bozena Czerny, John Lattanzio and Rolf |title=Astronomy and Astrophysics - Volume I |date=2012 |publisher=EOLSS Publications |isbn=978-1-78021-000-1 }}{{pn|date=February 2023}}</ref> His hypothesis was not widely circulated and did not get immediate attention at the time, but would later be independently reinvented and developed in detail in a 1969 article by [[Stirling Colgate]] and Chester McKee.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Colgate |first1=Stirling A. |last2=McKee |first2=Chester |title=Early Supernova Luminosity |journal=The Astrophysical Journal |date=August 1969 |volume=157 |pages=623 |doi=10.1086/150102 |bibcode=1969ApJ...157..623C }}</ref> In 2014, the first direct observational evidence for the theory was gathered, confirming Pankey's initial hypothesis.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Panther |first1=Fiona H |last2=Seitenzahl |first2=Ivo R |last3=Ruiter |first3=Ashley J |last4=Siegert |first4=Thomas |last5=Sim |first5=Stuart |last6=Crocker |first6=Roland M |title=Prospects of direct detection of 48V gamma-rays from thermonuclear supernovae |journal=Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society |date=5 October 2021 |volume=508 |issue=2 |pages=1590–1598 |doi=10.1093/mnras/stab2701 |doi-access=free |arxiv=2103.16840 }}</ref>

In 1957, while attending graduate school, Pankey began work at the [[United States Naval Research Laboratory]] as a research physicist and cosmologist. While at the Naval Research Laboratory, he worked with John E. Davey and published widely on material science and semi-conductor physics. The pair made significant contributions to [[molecular-beam epitaxy]] by demonstrating how to grow [[gallium arsenide]] films in vacuum chambers.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Davey |first1=John E. |last2=Pankey |first2=Titus |title=Epitaxial GaAs Films Deposited by Vacuum Evaporation |journal=Journal of Applied Physics |date=March 1968 |volume=39 |issue=4 |pages=1941–1948 |doi=10.1063/1.1656467 |bibcode=1968JAP....39.1941D }}</ref> The pair also submitted a patent for a method of forming gallium phosphide coatings in 1969.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Office |first=United States Patent |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=VaD5ctQMlZQC&dq=%22titus+pankey%22&pg=PA605 |title=Official Gazette of the United States Patent Office: Patents |date=1972 |publisher=The Office |language=en}}</ref> In 1977, Pankey and Richard E. Thomas submitted a patent for a controlled-porosity dispenser cathode.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Titus Pankey, Jr. Inventions, Patents and Patent Applications - Justia Patents Search |url=https://patents.justia.com/inventor/titus-pankey-jr |access-date=2023-04-25 |website=patents.justia.com}}</ref>

After completing his doctorate in 1962, Pankey became an associate professor of physics at [[Howard University]]. He taught at Howard until 1979, when he suffered a brain injury during a robbery and assault at his home in Washington, D.C. After recovering from the assault, he continued to conduct physics research at his home.

== Personal life ==
Pankey was married to Anita-Rae Smith-Pankey, and the couple later divorced. They had five children. Around 1980, he left Washington, D.C., and moved back to the [[Charlottesville, Virginia|Charlottesville]] area where he lived until his death.<ref name=":1">{{Cite news |title=Sydelle F. Corwin Real Estat ... |newspaper=Washington Post |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/local/2003/09/27/sydelle-f-corwin-real-estat/67e2edbc-5834-431f-9d3d-fd6aa6ba4330/ }}</ref>
